title: Consensus — Raft/Paxos basics
subtitle: How Replicated State Machines achieve linearizable fault-tolerant agreement using Raft Terms, Log Replication, and Quorum Safety.
keyTakeaways: Consensus algorithms (Raft, Multi-Paxos, ZAB) allow a cluster of `2f + 1` nodes to act as a single coherent Replicated State Machine, tolerating up to `f` node failures.
Raft decomposes consensus into three sub-problems: Leader Election (`RequestVote`), Log Replication (`AppendEntries`), and Safety (only nodes with all committed entries can win election).

Adding more nodes to a consensus group increases fault tolerance (5 nodes survive 2 failures vs 3 nodes surviving 1), but *decreases* write throughput because every write must replicate to more nodes.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Consensus — Raft/Paxos basics is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. How Replicated State Machines achieve linearizable fault-tolerant agreement using Raft Terms, Log Replication, and Quorum Safety. Fundamentally, Raft divides time into monotonically increasing logical **Terms** (acting as a logical clock). At any time, each node is in one of three states: **Leader**, **Follower**, or **Candidate**. Under normal operation, the Leader sends periodic `AppendEntries` heartbeats to Followers. If a Follower hears nothing within its randomized election timeout (`150ms–300ms`), it increments `currentTerm`, transitions to Candidate, votes for itself, and requests votes from peers via `RequestVote` RPCs.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Consensus algorithms (Raft, Multi-Paxos, ZAB) allow a cluster of `2f + 1` nodes to act as a single coherent Replicated State Machine, tolerating up to `f` node failures.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Raft decomposes consensus into three sub-problems: Leader Election (`RequestVote`), Log Replication (`AppendEntries`), and Safety (only nodes with all committed entries can win election).
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, consensus — raft/paxos basics manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **3-Node Raft / Paxos Group (Quorum = 2)**: Focuses on lowest write latency and network fan-out; tolerates 1 node failure. Best suited for Single-region high-speed consensus groups (etcd, Kafka KRaft, TiKV shards)..

**5-Node Raft / Paxos Group (Quorum = 3)**: Focuses on tolerates 2 simultaneous node failures; remains fault-tolerant even during rolling upgrades. Best suited for Mission-critical control planes, global metadata stores, and multi-region spanner deployments..
Randomized Election Timeouts: By picking a random timeout between 150ms and 300ms, almost always one node times out first and wins a majority before any peer wakes up—preventing split votes.

Two-Phase Log Commit (`AppendEntries`): When the Leader receives a write, it appends the entry to its local WAL (uncommitted) and sends `AppendEntries` to all Followers in parallel. Once a majority (`floor(N/2) + 1`) persist the entry, the Leader advances `commitIndex`, applies the command to its State Machine, and notifies Followers on the next heartbeat.

ReadIndex Optimization: The Leader records its current `commitIndex`, sends a lightweight heartbeat round to a majority of peers to confirm it is still the active Leader, waits until its state machine has applied at least `ReadIndex`, and serves the read without writing to the Raft log.

Leader Leases (Clock-Bounded): Using bounded clock drift (like Google Spanner's TrueTime or CockroachDB's Raft leases), the Leader serves local reads with 0 network hops while its lease is guaranteed not to have expired on peers.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around consensus — raft/paxos basics unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Single-region high-speed consensus groups (etcd, Kafka KRaft, TiKV shards). and environments requiring Lowest write latency and network fan-out; tolerates 1 node failure..

**Where to Use — High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Mission-critical control planes, global metadata stores, and multi-region spanner deployments. where Tolerates 2 simultaneous node failures; remains fault-tolerant even during rolling upgrades..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: A subtle trap in Raft: if a client sends a Read request to the Leader, can the Leader immediately return its local in-memory state? No! If the Leader was silently partitioned from the rest of the cluster 2 seconds ago, the other nodes may have already elected a new Leader in a higher Term and mutated the key. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, consensus — raft/paxos basics introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose during planned maintenance on 1 node, a single unexpected crash on the remaining 2 halts the group.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when higher network replication overhead and quorum commit latency.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering consensus — raft/paxos basics is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Adding more nodes to a consensus group increases fault tolerance (5 nodes survive 2 failures vs 3 nodes surviving 1), but *decreases* write throughput because every write must replicate to more nodes.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Never say 'We'll add more nodes to our ZooKeeper/etcd cluster to scale write throughput.' Consensus groups replicate *every* write to all nodes; to scale writes horizontally, partition the keyspace into multiple independent Raft groups ('Multi-Raft', used by CockroachDB and TiKV).
